text.p: Cigarette maker Rothmans Holdings Ltd said on Wednesday it expected a flat performance in the coming 12 months after earlier announcing a near doubling in net profit to A$94.73 million for the year to March 31, 1997.
"The next 12 month we think will be flat. The market is static or in some decline," general manager Gary Krell told reporters after the company released its 1996/97 results.

Rothmans described its net profit as a satisfying result, with the improvement due to a recovery by the Australian tobacco operations from the unprecedented price war which occurred during the previous year.
However Krell said pessimistic forecasts could be attributed to declines in the cigarette industry in general rather than the performance of individual companies.
"This is a very, very competitive industry and will continue to be," Krell told reporters.
Krell said competitive pricing between the three major tobacco companies might not again reach levels seen the previous year but added certain amounts of discounting must be expected.
"Pricing is a very, very sensitive issue but we will be defending our market share," he said.

One cause for optimism was the company's emerging market in Indonesia, where both total cigarette volumes and sales of Rothmans brands have increased. "We're mildly optimistic about our performance in Indonesia," Krell said.

Operating profit before interest, tax and abnormals for Australia was A$93.11 million, up from A$64.49 the previous year. Profits for the second half were lower than the first half mainly due to a lower result for the Australian operations owing to lower cigarette volume and price reductions on specific brands and increased general marketing costs.
Rothmans is about 50 percent owned by Rothmans International Ltd, which in turn is owned 60 percent by Swiss firm Richemont AG and 40 percent by South African group Rembrandt Group Ltd.
Despite the gloomy forecast Rothmans announced a final dividend of A$1.25, including a special A$1.00 dividend. The company paid a final dividend of 22 cents a year ago.

Krell said the special dividend came from the repatriation of retained earnings from Rothman's New Zealand operations. He added that, while the dividend was a significant amount, Rothmans retained enough money to fund expansion in Indonesia.
"I don't think the dividend hinders that," Krell said.
Rothmans shares hit an all-time high after the profit and dividend announcement, jumping 70 cents or 8.4 percent to close at A$9.00.
Volume at more than 232,000 shares was active for what is usually a lightly traded stock.
